definitions.definition: The doctrine that Brahman, qualified by souls and matter as its inseparable modes, is one without a second; also read as the non-duality of Brahman in its causal (subtle) and effected (gross) states.
A mode: an entity that exists only as the attribute of another (its prakārin) and cannot be known apart from it; souls and matter are modes of Brahman.
That which qualifies and distinguishes a substrate (viśeṣya); the soul is a qualifier of Brahman and so an 'aṃśa' of it.

Any substance that a conscious being wholly controls and supports for its own purposes and that exists for it alone (as its śeṣa); in this sense all souls and all matter are the body of the Lord, who is their self (śarīrin).

The relation of inseparable existence between a substance and its mode (as between Brahman and souls/matter, or a substance and its attribute): the mode can neither exist nor be known apart from the substrate, yet is distinct from it.

The application of several words, with different grounds of application, to one and the same object ('the blue lotus'); identity statements like 'tat tvam asi' name one Brahman under different modes, keeping the primary sense of each word.
The three real categories: cit (souls), acit (insentient matter) and Īśvara (the Lord).
Sentient reality: the individual souls, eternal, atomic knowers, bound, freed or eternally free; one of the three realities.
Insentient reality in three kinds: pure sattva, mixed sattva (prakṛti) and that devoid of sattva (time); the body of the Lord together with the souls.
Nārāyaṇa, the third reality: the self of all, cause of the world, opposed to all evil and abode of infinite auspicious qualities, present in five forms.
The supreme reality, Nārāyaṇa, great in essence and qualities and making others great; qualified (saviśeṣa) by souls and matter, never an attributeless consciousness.
The individual self: eternal, atomic, a knower by nature and possessing attributive consciousness, agent and enjoyer dependent on the Lord, essentially his servant (śeṣa); countless in number.

Attributive consciousness: the soul's (and the Lord's) consciousness as a quality distinct from the self-luminous substrate; eternal, it contracts in bondage through karma and expands fully in liberation; it goes out to objects as a lamp's light.
The self as what the word and awareness 'I' refer to; not the ego-evolute of prakṛti but the soul itself, which persists as 'I' in deep sleep and liberation.
The soul's atomic size: it dwells in the heart and pervades the body by its attributive consciousness.
That whose nature is to exist for the purpose of another (the śeṣin) and to enhance him; every soul and thing is śeṣa of the Lord.
The soul's essential nature as belonging to and existing for the Lord; its fulfilment is service (kainkarya).
The soul's being fit to belong to the Lord alone, not to itself nor to any other being; taught in the praṇava of the tirumantra.
Complete dependence on the Lord for existence, knowledge and action; the Teṅkalai hold it deeper than śeṣatva, excluding any independent act of one's own toward salvation.
The twofold character of Brahman in all scripture: opposition to all that is defiling and possession of infinite auspicious qualities.
Brahman's freedom from, and opposition to, every defect: ignorance, karma, change, suffering.

literal: opposed to all that is to be shunned

definitions.definition: The Lord's infinite, unsurpassed auspicious qualities — knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour and countless others such as compassion, accessibility and motherly love — not born of prakṛti.
The Lord's highest form in Vaikuṇṭha, seated with Śrī, Bhū and Nīlā, served by the eternal and freed souls.
The four emanations Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna and Aniruddha, each manifesting the six qualities or pairs of them, for creation, maintenance, dissolution and for the meditation of seekers.
The Lord's descents (avatāra) — principal ones like Rāma and Kṛṣṇa in bodies of pure sattva taken by his will, and secondary ones by empowerment of souls — for the protection of the good.
The Lord dwelling within every soul and thing as its self and controller, and, in a special form, in the heart of the meditator.
The Lord's descent into consecrated images in temples and homes, the most accessible of his forms, where he depends even on his worshippers.
The Lord's eternal domain, Vaikuṇṭha or Paramapada, made of pure sattva, beyond prakṛti and time, where the eternal and freed souls serve him.
The realm of prakṛti and time, where creation, maintenance and dissolution are the Lord's play and bound souls transmigrate.
A self-luminous insentient substance free of rajas and tamas, of which Vaikuṇṭha and the divine forms of the Lord and the freed are made.
Prakṛti, in which sattva is mixed with rajas and tamas; the material of bodies and worlds; it veils the soul's knowledge.
Time (kāla), the insentient reality lacking the guṇas, which measures change in the realm of prakṛti.
An eternal insentient substance without the guṇas, the Lord's body and instrument; in the eternal realm time exists but does not govern.
Mixed-sattva matter with the three guṇas, eternal and real, the Lord's body, transforming into the twenty-three evolutes; it is also called māyā because it produces wonderful effects.
Not an illusion-producing ignorance but prakṛti, called māyā because it produces manifold wonderful effects, and the Lord's wonderful power; the world it produces is real.

Not an indescribable cosmic ignorance but karma (the third power 'avidyā-karma' of Viṣṇu Purāṇa 6.7.61) and the ignorance it causes in the soul — the contraction of its knowledge and the mistaking of body for self.

Rāmānuja's seven objections to Advaita's avidyā: of locus (āśraya), concealment (tirodhāna), nature (svarūpa), indescribability (anirvacanīyatva), means of knowledge (pramāṇa), remover (nivartaka) and removal (nivṛtti).
The theory that every cognition, even erroneous, apprehends something real; error is incomplete apprehension, explained by the triplication of elements (silver-particles present in the shell).
Three are accepted — perception, inference and scripture; all of them apprehend qualified objects, none an undifferentiated reality.
Scriptural texts (such as the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa and Subāla Upaniṣad) that teach the body–self relation and so reconcile the texts of difference and of non-difference.
The real change of Brahman's body from subtle to gross in creation, Brahman as self remaining unchanged; opposed to Advaita's apparent transformation (vivarta).
The doctrine that the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā (on ritual) and the Uttara Mīmāṃsā (on Brahman), with the Saṅkarṣa-kāṇḍa, form one continuous science.
The name of the supreme as never apart from Śrī (Lakṣmī); the Lord is known and approached as her consort.
The proper name of the supreme Brahman: both the abode of all souls and things and the one who abides in them; Brahmā and Śiva are souls in his body.

literal: abode of the souls / in whom all abide

definitions.definition: The Lord as distinct from and higher than both the bound (kṣara) and the freed (akṣara) souls (Gītā 15.16–18).
The Lord's eternal consort, inseparable from him, mother of the world and mediator; her rank is disputed between the northern and southern schools.
All-pervading like Viṣṇu and of the Lord's rank; with him the means and the goal; the divine couple is the object of surrender.
The mediator (puruṣakāra) who reconciles soul and Lord; not herself the means; commonly reported as atomic in essence and of the rank of souls, though ever inseparable from the Lord.
The Lord as possessing the six qualities (knowledge, power, lordship, strength, virility, splendour) without limit.

literal: the one possessing the six excellences

definitions.definition: Souls bound in saṃsāra by beginningless karma, their knowledge contracted.
Souls released from saṃsāra who have reached Vaikuṇṭha and serve the Lord eternally.
Souls never bound, such as Ananta (Śeṣa), Garuḍa and Viṣvaksena, eternally serving the Lord in Vaikuṇṭha.
A bound soul seeking liberation — either the isolation of the self (kaivalya) or the Lord; the latter are bhaktas or prapannas.
The enjoyment of one's own pure self apart from the Lord, sought by some seekers; a lesser goal than the Lord's service.
Not permanent: those who attain it eventually go on to the Lord.
A permanent state, in a region at the edge of the eternal realm, from which there is no return.
The 'knowledge' the Upaniṣads enjoin for liberation: repeated, continuous meditation on Brahman, which, when it becomes loving and vivid, is bhakti.
Unbroken remembrance of the Lord flowing like a stream of oil, the form that liberating meditation takes (from Chāndogya 7.26.2, 'dhruvā smṛtiḥ').
The vividness that perfected meditation attains, equal to direct perception of the Lord.

literal: having the form of direct seeing

definitions.definition: Meditation that has become love: knowledge in the form of supreme affection (prīti) for the Lord, the means to liberation prescribed by the Upaniṣads.
The loving meditation of the Upaniṣads, the direct means to the Lord, prepared by karma-yoga and jñāna-yoga and supported by the seven aids.
Action according to one's duty, without sense of agency, ownership or desire for fruit, as the Lord's worship; it purifies the mind and itself can lead to the vision of the self.
Contemplation of the self as distinct from matter, leading to the vision of the self (ātmāvalokana), which prepares for bhakti.
The direct experience of one's own self as distinct from matter, the fruit of karma- and jñāna-yoga and prerequisite for bhakti-yoga.

Viveka (purity of food), vimoka (freedom from desire), abhyāsa (practice), kriyā (ritual duties), kalyāṇa (virtues), anavasāda (no dejection), anuddharṣa (no excessive elation) — the aids to meditation listed by the Vākyakāra.
The first of three states Rāmānuja prays for: intense longing that cannot bear separation, arising from knowledge of the Lord.
The second state: direct vision of the Lord granted to the one filled with parabhakti.
The third state: love so intense that separation from the vision would be unbearable; it ripens into attainment.
Surrender to the Lord (with Śrī) as one's sole refuge, the path of those who have no other means.
An independent means (upāya) performed once with its limbs, the occasion (vyāja) for the Lord's grace.
Not a means but the soul's acceptance of the Lord as the already-accomplished means, befitting its dependent nature.

equivalents.note: used interchangeably with śaraṇāgati, nyāsa and bharanyāsa

definitions.definition: The same as prapatti: surrender with the limbs of ānukūlya-saṅkalpa, prātikūlya-varjana, mahāviśvāsa, goptṛtva-varaṇa, kārpaṇya and ātma-nikṣepa.
The principal act of prapatti: placing the burden of one's protection and its fruit on the Lord; often performed through a teacher.
Giving oneself over to the Lord's protection — the principal (aṅgin) of prapatti in Deśika's account, the sixth of the six in the Ahirbudhnya verse.
The resolve to do only what pleases the Lord; first limb of prapatti.
Abstaining from what displeases the Lord; second limb of prapatti.
Firm faith that the Lord will certainly protect ('rakṣiṣyati'); third limb of prapatti and, for Deśika, the most essential.
Asking the Lord to be one's protector; fourth limb of prapatti.
The humble awareness of one's inability to adopt any other means; fifth limb of prapatti.
Destitution of any means of one's own — no ritual merit, self-knowledge or devotion — the qualification for surrender.
Having no other refuge or goal than the Lord; with ākiñcanya the qualification for surrender.
The means to liberation; the five in Arthapañcaka are karma, jñāna, bhakti, prapatti and the teacher's regard.
The goal: the Lord (with Śrī) himself and eternal service to him.

literal: goal, what is to be attained

definitions.definition: The Lord himself as the means, eternally existent and not produced by any act of the soul.
A means that the soul performs (bhakti-yoga, or — for the Vaṭakalai — prapatti) to win the Lord's grace.
The soul's act (surrender) that the Lord's free grace takes as its occasion so that he is not partial.
Śrī's role of intercession: she turns the soul toward the Lord and moves the Lord to forgive and receive it.
The Lord's grace as uncaused by any act of the soul.
The Lord as relishing, out of motherly love, the very faults of those who take refuge in him.

literal: one for whom faults are enjoyable

definitions.definition: The Lord's love that overlooks — or, for the Teṅkalai, relishes — the faults of the dependent, like a cow's for its calf.
The Lord's being the owner of all, which gives him the right and the will to save what is his.
The Lord's mixing freely with the lowly without regard to his greatness.
The Lord's easy reach, shown above all in his descents and in the temple image.
The Lord's compassion, personified by Deśika as a goddess in the Dayāśataka; the schools define it differently.
Śrī and Nārāyaṇa together as the one object of surrender and of service.
One who has performed (V) or accepted (T) surrender; he has done what is to be done and lives in service.
One who, unable to bear saṃsāra, asks for release at once, at the end of this body.
One who surrenders and waits until his begun karma is exhausted.
Seeking nothing from the Lord but the Lord himself and his service.
Before every act, relinquishing the sense of being its agent, the sense that it is one's own and desire for its fruit, attributing all to the Lord.

literal: relinquishment in the mode of goodness

definitions.definition: The scriptural duties as the Lord's commands, which the surrendered still obey (ājñā), and further services allowed but not required (anujñā).
Service to the Lord (and his devotees) that expresses the soul's nature as his śeṣa; the goal both here and in Vaikuṇṭha.
Being held as one's own by a true teacher, which the Śrīvacanabhūṣaṇam teaches is itself sufficient for salvation for one who can do nothing else.
The three mantras of the Śrīvaiṣṇava: the tirumantra (aṣṭākṣara), the dvaya and the carama-śloka (Gītā 18.66).
'Oṃ namo nārāyaṇāya', the eight-syllable root mantra, teaching the soul's exclusive belonging to the Lord and its prayer for service.
The two-sentence mantra of surrender: in the first the soul takes refuge at the feet of Nārāyaṇa with Śrī; in the second it prays for service to the divine couple.
Bhagavad Gītā 18.66, read as the Lord's command to surrender to him alone, with the promise of freedom from all sins.
In the tirumantra, a-u-m teach that the soul (m) exists for the Lord (a) alone (u).
Knowledge of the self, the Lord, the means, the goal and the obstacle — the content a seeker must learn from the teacher.

literal: the five things to be known

definitions.definition: The obstacles to liberation, fivefold: to knowing the self, the Lord's supremacy, the means, the goal, and to attainment.
The nine relations of Lord and soul: father–son, protector–protected, master–servant, husband–wife, knower–known, owner–owned, support–supported, self–body, enjoyer–enjoyed.
The true teacher (sadācārya) of the unbroken lineage, who imparts the five sacraments and the secret mantras out of compassion.
The lineage from the Lord and Śrī through Viṣvaksena, Nammāḻvār, Nāthamuni, Yāmuna and Rāmānuja, recited before study.
The Śrīvaiṣṇava initiation by the five sacraments, by which one becomes the teacher's disciple.
The Sanskrit Upaniṣads and the Tamil Prabandham (above all the Tiruvāymoḻi) as one Vedānta of equal authority.
The Āḻvārs' hymns (Divya Prabandham) as graciously given; the Tamil Veda.
The Tamil–Sanskrit mixed idiom of the Śrīvaiṣṇava commentaries and rahasya works.
A verse of homage to a teacher or text recited before the Prabandham and the teachers' works.
The 108 temples sung by the Āḻvārs (106 on earth, with the Milky Ocean and Vaikuṇṭha), where the Lord abides in his image form.
Praying for the Lord's well-being out of love, as the Āḻvārs did, instead of asking anything for oneself.
Offence against the Lord's devotees, including judging them by birth — graver than offence against the Lord.
Expiation for deliberate offences after surrender, which the Vaṭakalai require (or a renewed surrender) and the Teṅkalai do not regard as needed for salvation.
Sins before the attainment of knowledge or surrender, which are destroyed, and those after it, which do not cling (if unintentional).
Karma that has begun to bear fruit in the present body and is exhausted by experiencing it; for the surrendered the Lord may end it at once.
Remembering the Lord at the moment of death; required of the bhakti-yogin but not of the surrendered, whom the Lord remembers.
The path of the gods by which the freed soul travels from the body to Vaikuṇṭha, escorted by the deities of light, day, the bright fortnight, the northern course, the year and the rest.
The deities who conduct the departed soul along the path of light.
The superhuman being who, at the lightning, leads the soul to Brahman.
The river at the boundary of prakṛti and the eternal realm; crossing it the soul sheds its subtle body.
The eternal realm of the Lord, made of pure sattva, the goal of the freed.
Release from karma and saṃsāra after the fall of the body, reaching Vaikuṇṭha and eternally serving the Lord, with individuality kept and knowledge fully expanded.
Liberation as the manifestation, not the creation, of the soul's own nature, freed from karma.
The freed soul's equality with Brahman in the enjoyment of bliss, not in cosmic function.
The freed share all the Lord's powers except creating, sustaining and ruling the world (BS 4.4.17).
Rejected: while the body lasts karma remains; liberation comes only when the body falls.
The image, attached to the Vaṭakalai, of the baby monkey that clings to its mother: the soul must make the act of surrender.

literal: the maxim of the young monkey
notes: Label used in the dispute literature and modern accounts; the schools' own texts argue in other terms.

definitions.definition: The image, attached to the Teṅkalai, of the kitten carried by the mother cat: the Lord saves without the soul's effort.
A member of the community of Rāmānuja's tradition, worshipping Nārāyaṇa with Śrī.
Tamil names of the Lord (Viṣṇu) in the temples; Rāmānuja is 'Emperumāṉār', 'the one who is (like) our Lord'.
The Śrīvaiṣṇava's customary way of saying 'I', expressing servitude.
The vertical forehead mark of white clay with the central line (śrīcūrṇa) for Śrī; U-shaped among the Vaṭakalai, Y-shaped with a line down the nose among the Teṅkalai.
The hereditary temple performance of the Prabandham in song, gesture and dance by the araiyars, traced to Nāthamuni.
The title of Śrīvaiṣṇava renouncers who head maṭhas (Vānamāmalai, Ahobilam, Parakāla and others).
Traditional study of the Śrībhāṣya, Gītābhāṣya, the Tiruvāymoḻi commentaries and the rahasyas at the feet of a teacher.
Dream, whose objects the Lord creates for the dreamer to experience minor fruits of karma.
Deep sleep, in which the self rests in the Lord in the heart with knowledge contracted, persisting as 'I'.
The Lord's real descent in a body of pure sattva by his own will, not from karma.
An evolute of prakṛti; distinct from the true 'I' (aham-artha), which is the self; the false identification of body as self is the obstacle.
